entry.title: GIS Trend 1
entry.content:
From mapping places to understanding patterns

Geographic information systems (GIS) have long helped us organize, map, and analyze information tied to locations.

GIS trend from the history

Figure: Sikder et al. (2025), full paper

GIS is evolving beyond traditional desktop-based workflows and map-centric interfaces. The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) has introduced a new paradigm: Conversational GIS, where users can interact with spatial data, query geospatial services, and perform analyses using natural language.

But the next step is already taking shape: Agentic GIS.

While Conversational GIS focuses on understanding user instructions and translating them into spatial operations, Agentic GIS goes further. It enables AI agents to plan workflows, select appropriate tools, execute geoprocessing tasks, interpret results, and iteratively refine analyses with limited human intervention.

This transition marks a shift in how we interact with geospatial technologies:

Traditional GIS: Users operate tools and configure workflows.

Conversational GIS: Users describe tasks; AI translates them into GIS operations.

Agentic GIS: Users define objectives; AI agents plan, execute, evaluate, and coordinate workflows.

The underlying transformation is not simply about adding chat interfaces to GIS. It is about connecting LLMs with geospatial data infrastructures, APIs, processing engines, knowledge graphs, and interoperable standards such as OGC APIs.

One Thing: human oversight, reproducibility, data provenance, and transparent decision-making remain essential, particularly for complex spatial analyses.

The emerging question is no longer just how we can talk to GIS, but how GIS agents can autonomously reason and act on spatial data to support evidence-based decisions. We, GIS practioners and professions need to think critical but responsible how to shape the future.
entry.summary: How artificial intelligence and machine learning are expanding the ways we analyze geographic data.

entry.title: marimo notebook in python nativ
entry.content:
marimo notebooks can run Python directly in the reader’s browser. Opt a page in from its front matter:

---
layout: post
title: a post with marimo snippets
marimo: true
---

Nothing is loaded on pages without that flag, so bundling the plugin costs nothing site-wide.

Runnable snippets

Wrap fenced Python blocks in a container and the runtime turns them into an interactive notebook after the page loads:

import marimo as mo

slider = mo.ui.slider(1, 20, value=5, label="n")
slider

mo.md(f"The first {slider.value} squares: {[i**2 for i in range(1, slider.value + 1)]}")

Until the runtime has moved those blocks into place the container stays hidden, so readers never see the raw source flash before it becomes a notebook.

Embedding a hosted notebook

If you already publish a notebook — on marimo.app or your own WASM host — embed it instead:

{% al_marimo_embed src="https://marimo.app/l/your-notebook" height="700px" caption="Sampling demo" %}

The frame is sandboxed without allow-same-origin, so the embedded notebook cannot reach this page’s storage or cookies.

A note on what this loads

The marimo-snippets runtime is vendored into the plugin at a pinned version and served from your own site, rather than pulled from a CDN — so no third-party origin executes script in your readers’ pages. Running a notebook does contact marimo’s host, which is worth knowing before you opt a page in.
entry.summary: running Python in the browser with marimo
